\chapter{Deriving the Rest}
\label{ch:spanish-derive-plurals}
\hlchaptermodality{76}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can produce the plural of any irregular verb in this book from rules, and conjugate a verb I was never shown.}

Three rules generate the whole present tense - and a system, unlike a table, works on words it has never seen.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[queremos · quieren]{queremos, quieren — work them out first}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-plurales-cambio}



\begin{quote}
Before you read on: you have the singular of \emph{querer}, and you have the stem-change rule. \textbf{What is \textquotedblleft{}we want\textquotedblright{}?} Say your answer out loud, then continue.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you were right}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{queremos} — \emph{we want.}  ·  \textbf{quieren} — \emph{they want.} \textbf{podemos} — \emph{we can.}  ·  \textbf{pueden} — \emph{they can.}
\end{quote}

If you said \emph{queremos} rather than \emph{quieremos}, you did not remember it. You \textbf{derived} it, from a rule you were given one chapter ago: the stem breaks exactly where it is stressed, so \emph{nosotros} never breaks.

And \emph{quieren} breaks, because there the stress is back on the stem.

That is the difference between a course that hands you tables and one that hands you rules. Four forms you had never seen, and none of them needed teaching.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A test you can run yourself.} You have \emph{puedo} and \emph{puedes}. Without being told, what are \emph{we can} and \emph{they can}?
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \emph{yo}, \emph{nosotros} and \emph{ellos} forms of \emph{querer} — break, no break, break
  \item the same three for \emph{poder}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we want\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Queremos}.) Why no break? (The stress is on the \textbf{ending}.) And could you have produced these without this lesson? (\textbf{Yes} — which is the point of it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hacemos · hacen]{hacemos, hacen — and the club has no plural at all}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-plurales-yo-go}



\begin{quote}
Name the six \emph{-go} verbs. And say where in each one the \emph{-go} appears.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an oddity that was only ever in one slot}]
You were told, when the club closed, that the \textbf{-go} lives in the \emph{yo} form and nowhere else. Here is what that is worth:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hacemos} · \textbf{hacéis} · \textbf{hacen} — plain \emph{-er} endings. \textbf{ponemos} · \textbf{ponéis} · \textbf{ponen} — plain \emph{-er} endings. \textbf{salimos} · \textbf{salís} · \textbf{salen} — plain \emph{-ir} endings.
\end{quote}

Nothing to learn. The \emph{-go} club has no plural forms of its own, because the thing that made it a club was never in the plural to begin with.

Two of the six do something in the plural, and it is \textbf{not} the \emph{-go}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{decimos} but \textbf{dicen} · \textbf{venimos} but \textbf{vienen}
\end{quote}

Those are stem changes, and they follow the rule you already have — the stem breaks where it is stressed, and \emph{nosotros} is never stressed on the stem. So even the exceptions are not exceptions.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two rules — \textbf{the \emph{-go} is yo-only}, and \textbf{stems break under stress} — now generate the entire present tense of every irregular verb in this book, in every person.

That is what a rule buys that a table does not: the table stops at the forms printed on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six \emph{-go} verbs in the \emph{we} form — and hear that none is odd
  \item \textquotedblleft{}decimos, dicen\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}venimos, vienen\textquotedblright{} — the two that break, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many special plural forms does the \emph{-go} club have? (\textbf{None} — the \emph{-go} was only ever in \emph{yo}.) Which two do something in the plural, and what? (\emph{Decir} and \emph{venir} — a \textbf{stem change}, following the stress.) How many rules now generate every irregular present in this book? (\textbf{Two}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Synthesis — a verb you have never met}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-sintesis-derivar}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter, and nothing to memorise. Say the six endings of a regular \emph{-er} verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Everything you hold about the present tense now fits in three lines:

1. \textbf{Three families}, six endings each; \texttt{-er} and \texttt{-ir} differ only in \emph{nosotros} and \emph{vosotros}. 2. \textbf{A stem breaks exactly where it is stressed} — so \emph{nosotros} and \emph{vosotros} never break. 3. \textbf{A \texttt{-go} sits in the \emph{yo} form and nowhere else.}

That is the whole system. Not a summary of it — the system.

And a system, unlike a table, works on words it has never seen.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Here is a verb this book has not taught you: \textbf{beber}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink\textquotedblright{} — you have met the word, but never its full set.

Do not look anything up. It is a regular \texttt{-er} verb, so:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{bebo} · \textbf{bebes} · \textbf{bebe} · \textbf{bebemos} · \textbf{bebéis} · \textbf{beben}
\end{quote}

Six forms, and the only thing you needed was rule 1.

Now one that uses all three rules. \textbf{Salir} is an \texttt{-ir} verb, and it is in the \texttt{-go} club. Rules 1 and 3 give you every form, and you can produce them before reading on:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{salgo} · \textbf{sales} · \textbf{sale} · \textbf{salimos} · \textbf{salís} · \textbf{salen}
\end{quote}

One odd form, in the one slot rule 3 names. The other five are plain \texttt{-ir}.

Four broken, two whole, and the two whole ones are the two the stress leaves alone. Every time.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six of \emph{beber}, without looking
  \item all six of \emph{salir}, and name the only odd one
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until deriving is faster than remembering.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
State the three rules. (\textbf{Three families · stems break under stress · the -go is yo-only}.) Which two forms never break? (\emph{Nosotros}, \emph{vosotros}.) And what can you do now that a table could not give you? (\textbf{Conjugate a verb nobody taught me}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
